title: AI Decision Record (AIDR)
description: A record of one consequential AI-assisted output: what was asked, what the model relied on, how confident it was, where the data went, and whether a human reviewed it. Written at decision time, not reconstructed later.

allOf.description: reasoning_summary, confidence and limitations are model judgements. Every record requires them EXCEPT one written purely by a capture layer (attestation.method = application_captured), which cannot assess them and must not invent them. Records with no attestation — including all v0.1 records — still require them.
timestamp is required unless a capture-only record genuinely had no runtime-supplied time to record. Any self-reported or hybrid record must carry one.

aidr_version.description: Version of this schema the record conforms to. 0.1 records stay valid; 0.2 adds the optional 'trace' and 'attestation' fields.

id.description: Unique identifier for this record. UUID or any collision-free scheme.

timestamp.description: When the output was produced, ISO 8601 with timezone.

system.description: Which AI system produced this output. Should reference a system card.

name.description: Internal name of the deployed system, e.g. 'support-assistant'.

provider.description: Legal entity providing the model, e.g. 'Anthropic PBC'.

model.description: Model identifier as reported by the provider.

model_version.description: Version or snapshot, where the provider exposes one.

system_card.description: Path or URL to the system card for this system.

purpose.description: What this AI output was for, in plain language. An affected person should understand it.

input_summary.description: What was asked and what context was supplied. Summarise; do not copy personal data into the record.

output_summary.description: What the AI produced or recommended.

data_recipients.description: Every party that received data in the course of producing this output. GDPR Art. 13(1)(e), 15(1)(c). An empty array means the model ran entirely on infrastructure you control; state that explicitly rather than omitting recipients.

server_region.description: Where processing took place, e.g. 'US', 'EU (eu-central-1, Frankfurt)', 'on-premise'.

data_categories.description: Categories of data transferred, e.g. 'customer name', 'support ticket text'. Flag GDPR Art. 9 special categories explicitly.

transfer_mechanism.description: Legal basis for a third-country transfer, e.g. 'SCCs (2021/914)', 'adequacy decision', 'not applicable — EU processing'.

retention.description: How long the processor keeps it, e.g. '30 days abuse monitoring', 'zero retention'.

reasoning_summary.description: How the output was reached, in terms a non-specialist can follow. This is a self-report, not a faithful account of the model's internal computation — see the honest-limits note in the README.

trace.description: The steps taken to reach the output, in order. Each step is marked with its provenance: 'system_observed' means a capture layer logged the event as it happened; 'self_reported' means the model is describing it. A trace is required (by the skill, not the schema) whenever the output used tools or retrieval — where there are steps, they must be shown. See docs/design/2026-07-25-audit-trail-v0.2.md.

at.description: When this step happened, ISO 8601. Required in practice for system_observed steps; a self_reported step may not have a reliable time.

type.description: What kind of step this was.

provenance.description: 'system_observed': a capture layer logged this actual event. 'self_reported': the model's own account, not independently grounded. A step that cannot state which it is defeats the purpose of the trace.

summary.description: What happened at this step, in plain language. Summarise; never copy personal data in.

refs.description: Identifiers for what this step touched or produced — a query, a document id, a tool result reference. Not the data itself.

attestation.description: How this record came to exist, so an inspector need not infer its trust tier. Answers the first audit question: did your system capture this, or did the model write it about itself?

method.description: 'model_self_report': the model emitted the whole record (tier 1). 'application_captured': a capture layer built it from observed events. 'hybrid': observed steps plus model-supplied reasoning/confidence/limitations.

captured_by.description: The capture layer that wrote it, e.g. 'glassbox-hook@0.2 (claude-code)'. Empty for a bare self-report — and that emptiness is itself informative.

created_at.description: When the record was assembled, ISO 8601.

sources.description: What the output actually relied on: documents, records, retrieved passages, tool results.

type.description: 'model_knowledge' means it came from training data and is not independently verifiable.

confidence.description: How reliable this output is. 'level' is required; 'rationale' explains it.

rationale.description: Why this level. What would raise or lower it.

limitations.description: What this output does not cover, what could make it wrong, what was assumed. An empty array asserts there are none — rarely true. State at least one limitation or justify the emptiness in reasoning_summary.

human_review.description: Whether a human checked this before it took effect. Central to AI Act Art. 14 and 26(2), the Art. 50(4) editorial-review exemption, and GDPR Art. 22.

required.description: Whether human review was required before this output could take effect.

reason.description: Why review was or was not required.

reviewer.description: Who reviewed. A role plus an identifier, not just 'a manager'.

decision.description: Outcome. A record emitted at generation time carries 'pending' — the review has not happened yet, and the model must never write anything else here. The reviewer replaces it with the real outcome, adding reviewer and timestamp. If every completed record in your store says 'approved', that is a rubber-stamp signal, not a clean sheet — see gdpr-mapping.md.

decision_notes.description: What the reviewer changed or why they agreed.

affected_persons.description: Whether this output affects identifiable people, and whether they were told. Drives AI Act Art. 26(11) and 86, and GDPR Art. 22.

notified.description: Whether affected persons were informed that AI was involved.

explanation_available.description: Whether an Art. 86 explanation can be produced on request.

disclosure.description: Which AI Act Art. 50 disclosures were made for this interaction.

ai_interaction_disclosed.description: Art. 50(1) — the person was told they were dealing with AI.

risk_classification.description: AI Act risk class of the system producing this output.

retention_until.description: When this record may be deleted, ISO 8601. AI Act Art. 26(6) requires at least six months for high-risk system logs; other laws may require longer.

prev_record_hash.description: SHA-256 of the previous record in the chain, hex-encoded. Optional tamper-evidence — see logging-guide.md.
